findings.title: Named mercy at the opening legal boundary
findings.claim: The basmala's name and paired mercy epithets frame the opening legal distinctions as bounded access under a publicly invoked, protective authority: Allah's name is said over the trained catch, while the forced-hunger exception gives mercy a concrete edge.
findings.mechanism: The focus noun ism carries the name/designation relation and the two divine mercy epithets carry active protection and beneficence. Ayah 5:4 repeats Allah's name in a rule about what trained animals hold; 5:3 pairs a prohibition with an allowance for forced hunger and calls Allah merciful. Their contact turns the opening designation into a frame that operates within the rules.
findings.reader_payoff: The reader can see the opening formula at work in the first food boundaries: permission and restraint remain distinct, while necessity and the named act of consumption are handled within the stated divine order.
findings.containment: This does not claim that the basmala states every later rule, that every prohibition yields to need, or that pronouncing the name alone changes the catch's legal status. The specific restrictions and allowances remain as stated in their ayat.

epistemic.reason: The focus words and the 5:3-4 contexts are direct; treating them as a governing frame is an interpretation, bounded here to the opening legal cluster.

findings.title: Mercy across kinship and community
findings.claim: The mercy words can be heard through kinship and womb imagery: the mother-child scene lends them embodied texture, while a brother's murder opens into a rule treating one life as humanity's concern and an oath expiation measures aid to the poor against one's own household food. With food-sharing and alliance rules, the opening can make law feel relational rather than merely classificatory.
findings.mechanism: The focus epithets carry the root's mercy field. Ayat 5:30-32 move from a brother's death to a statement about the weight of any human life; 5:89 measures feeding the poor against what one feeds one's household; 5:5 and 5:51-82 regulate food, marriage, alliance, and intercommunity closeness. Ayah 5:75 presents Jesus with his mother Mary in an embodied human scene. These distinct contexts contact the kinship and womb branches without turning the focus epithets into their literal glosses.
findings.reader_payoff: The reader can perceive care for people beyond one's household as carrying the closeness associated with kin, while the mother-child scene gives the mercy image a bodily, life-bearing resonance.
findings.containment: Kinship and womb are contextual analogies alongside the ordinary mercy reading. This does not make every community tie a blood relation, claim that the epithets literally mean kinship or womb, or assign gender or a body to God.

epistemic.reason: The brother, family-feeding, intercommunity, and mother-child contexts are explicit; extending the womb branch from motherhood to the focus is analogical and is stated with that limit.

branch_activations.independent_trigger: Ayah 5:30 names the victim as a brother, 5:32 extends the weight of one life to all people, 5:89 uses household food as a measure for feeding the poor, and 5:5 and 5:51-82 address food, marriage, alliances, and relations between communities.
branch_activations.activation: The brother and household ties meet rules that reach beyond immediate kin; the kinship branch makes the focus's mercy read as connecting otherwise separate legal persons.
branch_activations.resulting_reading: Mercy can frame the law as relation-preserving, with obligations toward outsiders measured through the nearness of family ties.
branch_activations.boundary: This is an analogy from kinship to broader legal relations; the focus epithets do not literally name blood relatives.

branch_activations.boundary: The surah does not describe pregnancy here; this is an analogy from motherhood, not a claim that the focus adjective means womb or that God has a body.

findings.title: The name closed by dominion

findings.mechanism: The focus names Allah through ism; at 5:120 the surah closes by locating the heavens, earth, and whatever is in them within Allah's ownership and power. The branch's raised-designation image can meet that final scope, so the name at the opening is heard against the full domain named at the end.
findings.reader_payoff: The last ayah lets the reader return to the opening name with the full field of rules and stories in view, seeing their boundaries within a wider ownership.
findings.containment: This is a closing frame, not a claim that every individual rule exhausts divine dominion or that ism literally means sky or sovereignty.

epistemic.reason: The final ownership statement is explicit; its retrospective effect on the opening designation is an interpretive macro relation.

The specific naming act meets the focus word in its legal context and turns designation from label into practice.
findings.reader_payoff: The reader sees the opening name touch an ordinary act of obtaining food rather than remain only a formula before the law.
findings.containment: This does not say that the catch was otherwise forbidden or that naming alone confers permissibility; the interpretation stays within the rule stated in 5:4.

epistemic.reason: Ayah 5:4 directly supplies the repeated name and food act; the transfer from label to public designation is interpretive.

findings.title: The named one as the one worshipped
findings.claim: Because the surah explicitly commands worship of Allah and asks whether anything besides Allah is being worshipped, the opening proper name can be heard as the name of the one toward whom that act is directed; invocation and worship meet in the chapter's account.
findings.mechanism: The focus carries Allah's proper name. Ayat 5:72, 5:76, and 5:117 independently state that Allah is to be worshipped and reject worship directed elsewhere. The same named referent connects the opening invocation to the surah's explicit devotional act.
findings.reader_payoff: The opening reads as an orientation toward the one worshipped as well as a naming of authority before the legal material.
findings.containment: The focus remains a proper name in construct, not a generic word meaning deity or worship. The worship branch is activated through the named referent and later context, not by changing the focus's grammatical form.

epistemic.reason: The worship contexts are explicit, but the branch registry excludes pure proper-name uses; this is a referent-based contextual resonance with that restriction stated.

findings.title: The invocation beside legal oaths
findings.claim: The surah's rules for sworn testimony let the opening bi-ismi Allah carry a restrained oath-like resonance: the name invoked at the start later becomes the ground on which witnesses affirm truthful testimony.
findings.mechanism: The focus includes the divine proper name in a by-name phrase. In 5:106-108 witnesses swear by Allah, their testimony is tested, and further oaths are anticipated. The repeated named authority and the opening bi- relation connect invocation with a later binding speech act.
findings.reader_payoff: The opening name acquires a solemn relation to truthful testimony and the legal handling of speech.
findings.containment: The basmala is not itself a witness oath: it contains no sworn proposition or following negation, and the later testimony has its own form. The reading is a contextual echo through the named authority.

epistemic.reason: The oaths and their use of Allah's name are explicit; their return to the focus is contextual because the focus is an invocation rather than a sworn proposition.

findings.title: A verbal designation beside marked animals
findings.claim: The opening name can be heard as a verbal marker of status beside the surah's visible markers: its food rules protect garlanded animals and also require Allah's name over what trained animals catch.
findings.mechanism: The focus noun ism carries an identifying designation. Ayat 5:2 and 5:97 name al-qalaid among the protected offerings; 5:4 attaches Allah's name to a caught animal. The verbal name and visible garland meet in the surah's handling of recognized, protected animals.
findings.reader_payoff: The reader notices naming as one of the acts by which the chapter makes status and proper handling visible.
findings.containment: This is an analogy between a verbal designation and a visible animal marker. The focus word does not literally mean branding, and a garland is not the same act as the named instruction in 5:4.

epistemic.reason: The garlands and naming instruction are explicit; their relation to the physical-mark branch is analogical rather than a lexical reading of the focus.
